newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: China president arrives in Pakistan to cement ties.
newsitem.headline: China president arrives in Pakistan to cement ties.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin arrived on Sunday in Pakistan, the second stop on a regional tour Pakistani analysts said held out a long-term hope of helping to ease tensions on the fractious sub-continent.
Jiang flew in from India, Pakistan's arch rival, where the two Asian giants signed an agreement aimed at reducing tensions along their Himalayan border, site of a brief border war in 1962.
Analysts in Pakistan, whose relations with Beijing have been close for 30 years, applauded the pact, saying good relations between India and China should benefit the whole region.

"There is a perception in Pakistan that the developing relationship between India and China may impact adversely on China-Pakistan relations," said Nishat Ahmad, head of the Institute of Regional Studies think tank.
"My evaluation is that nothing of the sort is likely. If anything, it will have a moderating influence on India-Pakistan relations," he told Reuters.

"You can only positively influence another country if it sees you in cooperative mode. If China-India relations improve and there is trouble between Pakistan and India, that will give China the opportunity to help moderate the problem," he said.
"In fact, the understanding on the border issue is also a positive development and could be used as a model for a pact between India and Pakistan in certain respects," Ahmad added.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947 and Islamabad has leaned heavily on Chinese support.

New Delhi believes that includes supplies of missiles and nuclear technology, which Islamabad and Beijing deny. India, which denies having built atomic bombs despite setting off a nuclear explosion in 1974, has its own missile programme.
Diplomats in both capitals say they believe another war could go nuclear, however, and Indo-Pakistani relations are poor.

Analysts and diplomats said Jiang's visit was intended to demonstrate Beijing's commitment to its close ties with Islamabad and to begin using its improved relations with New Delhi to ease tensions on the sub-continent.

"Chinese foreign policy is basically orientated towards stablity. Economic development is their highest priority and for that they need peace and stability," said Akram Zaki, a former Pakistani ambassador to China.
"They are seeking a normalisation with India and a reduction of tensions generally. They don't want anyone to rock the boat," he said.
"This should be of no concern to Pakistan which must also concentrate on economic development and needs an environment of peace."

During Jiang's visit, Pakistan and China will sign a series of minor agreements, including one to keep open Islamabad's consulate in Hong Kong after Beijing takes back control of the British colony at the end of June next year, officials said.

They said another would allow Islamabad to open a consulate in Shanghai and a third would boost cooperation on cutting drug smuggling routes from Pakistan to Central Asia through the Chinese province of Sinkiang, an increasing problem.
They will also sign an agreement to set up a commercial panel to boost trade, which is very small by world standards because neither produces much the other needs to buy.
Jiang leaves on Wednesday for Nepal, the third and last stop on his regional tour.
